content: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is characterized by the sudden and unexplained death of an infant, typically occurring without any prior symptoms. It most commonly affects infants between the ages of one month and one year in the United States. Women who have experienced the loss of an infant due to SIDS are at a significantly increased risk of encountering complications in subsequent pregnancies. These complications include placenta previa, a condition where the placenta partially or completely covers the cervix; abruptio placenta, which involves the premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall; and premature rupture of membranes, where the amniotic sac breaks before labor begins. The prognosis for SIDS can vary depending on the presence of certain risk factors. These include a history of apparent life-threatening events (ALTE), which are episodes of sudden and alarming changes in an infant's breathing, color, or muscle tone. Additionally, a history of multiple concerning events prior to hospital admission and the presence of viral infections can significantly influence the prognosis in cases of SIDS.
